inputs.need:
I manage the tuberculosis program at a city public health unit that serves about 900,000 people. Each year we notify about 110 cases of pulmonary TB, and our nurses identify roughly 1,300 contacts who need evaluation: a symptom check, an interferon-gamma release assay or skin test, and a chest X-ray if anything is positive. Last year only 71 percent of identified contacts completed evaluation within 60 days, against a provincial target of 90 percent, and completion was lowest for household contacts who work shifts, contacts living in shelters, and contacts who need an interpreter.

The pathway has a lot of steps and handoffs: the case nurse visits the case and lists contacts, a second nurse phones each contact, the contact goes to one of three clinics for blood work, results come back to a central office, positives are booked for X-ray at the hospital, and then someone has to close the loop. People fall out at every step. We want to use Lean methods: map the value stream from case notification to completed contact evaluation, measure where the time and the drop-outs are, and redesign the flow, for example by drawing blood at the first home visit, sending results straight to the case nurse, and booking the X-ray at the same visit.

I need help deciding what to measure and how often, how to show real change with only about 110 cases a year, how to avoid making things worse for the contacts who are already hardest to reach, and how to get the data out of our case management system without months of manual abstraction.
inputs.constraints: No new staff. The case management system can export monthly reports; ad hoc queries need the data steward's approval. Contact names must stay within the TB program.

The data steward approved a monthly de-identified extract of contact evaluation dates from the case management system on 2026-09-12 (approval DS-114).
Three community clinics draw blood for contact testing; results reach the central TB office by fax or courier.

records.title: The contact evaluation cascade for pulmonary tuberculosis in a metropolitan health department
records.authors: Oyelaran-Whitfield J, Castellanos-Mbeki R, Lindahl-Osei P
records.abstract: Of 3,120 contacts identified for 262 pulmonary tuberculosis cases in one metropolitan health department, 88 percent were located, 79 percent had a test, and 68 percent completed evaluation. The largest losses occurred between a positive test and the chest radiograph, and among contacts living in shelters or working night shifts. Median time from contact identification to completed evaluation was 38 days. Contacts evaluated at home completed more often than those referred to clinics. The authors recommend reporting every step of the cascade rather than a single completion figure.

records.title: Blood draw at the first home visit for tuberculosis contacts: a program report
records.authors: City tuberculosis control program, Brackenmoor health unit
records.abstract: The program began drawing blood for interferon-gamma release assays at the first home visit instead of referring contacts to a clinic. The report states that completion of testing rose from 74 to 91 percent after the change, and that nurses spent more time per visit. It gives no dates for the before and after periods, no denominators by contact type and no information on whether chest radiographs were completed. Staff comments describe fewer lost samples once courier pickup was arranged.

records.title: Lean redesign of latent tuberculosis evaluation in a public health clinic
records.abstract: A public health clinic mapped the value stream of contact evaluation and found 11 handoffs between identification and completed evaluation. After redesign (same-day testing, results routed to the case nurse, radiograph booked at the result visit), median days from contact identification to completed evaluation fell from 41 to 19, and completion within 60 days rose from 66 to 82 percent over 12 months. Nurse time per contact rose slightly, and staff reported fewer calls chasing results. The comparison was before and after, with no concurrent control.

records.title: Interpreter use and completion of tuberculosis contact evaluation: an internal review
records.abstract: This internal review of one year of contact investigations found that contacts who needed an interpreter completed evaluation in 58 percent of cases, against 77 percent of other contacts. Telephone interpreters were used for most phone calls, but not at clinic visits for blood draws. The review does not give its year, and it did not adjust for household status, shelter residence or distance to the clinic. It recommends booking interpreters for every step, not only the first call, and recording each contact's preferred language at the first contact.

records.title: Interventions to improve completion of tuberculosis contact investigation: a systematic review
records.authors: Rasmussen-Oduya E, Petit-Kowalczyk M, Sato-Brennan L, Varga-Okafor D
records.abstract: We included 22 studies of interventions to improve completion of contact investigation, including home-based testing, incentives, text reminders and case management. Home-based testing and incentives raised completion by a median of 12 percentage points compared with usual care, while reminders alone had small effects. Most studies were before-and-after comparisons. Few studies reported outcomes for people experiencing homelessness or for contacts needing an interpreter, the groups with the lowest completion in most programs. Studies of testing in shelters were small and short, and none followed contacts beyond 90 days.

records.title: Measuring contact evaluation completion from case management systems: a data quality study
records.abstract: We compared case management system records with paper files for 600 tuberculosis contacts. Evaluation dates were missing for 14 percent of evaluations in the system but present on paper, most often chest radiograph dates entered by hospital staff. Completion estimated from the system alone was 9 percentage points lower than from paper files. A monthly extract with a data dictionary and a missing-date check reduced the gap to 2 points within three months. The check took about two hours of staff time a month.

records.title: Statistical process control for public health programs with small monthly counts
records.authors: Halvorsen-Quist B, Obi-Lindgren C, Reid-Nakashima V
records.abstract: Public health programs often chart outcomes with small monthly subgroups. We show that p-charts with monthly subgroups under 30 give wide, unstable limits, while grouping contacts into cohorts by the month the index case was notified and charting completion at a fixed interval gives stable subgroups of about 100 in a mid-sized program. Run chart rules detected a sustained 12-point improvement within five to six monthly cohorts in simulations. Cohorts must be closed only after the full follow-up interval has passed.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two undated program reports keep unknown relevance and method quality and stay unrated. Contact cascades lose most people between a positive test and the radiograph and among people in shelters or on night shifts. A Lean redesign elsewhere halved the time to completed evaluation and raised 60-day completion from 66 to 82 percent, and home-based testing is the best supported single change. System data miss evaluation dates unless checked. Cohort charts by index-case month suit a program of this size.
response.gradeRationale: Before-and-after improvement reports, a review of mostly uncontrolled studies and two unratable program reports; consistent direction, low certainty on effect size.
response.summary: Seven records appraised; two undated reports keep null scores and stay unrated; five claims.

response.reading: Each handoff in the pathway (case nurse, second nurse, clinic, central office, hospital) is a queue where contacts wait and some are lost. The biggest leak elsewhere is between a positive test and the radiograph, and the hardest-to-reach contacts leak most. Moving the blood draw into the first home visit and routing results to the case nurse remove two handoffs. Measurement depends on a system that misses dates unless checked.

response.overview: Lean improvement project in the TB program: two value stream mapping days in November 2026 with nurses, clinic staff, the central office and hospital radiology, then redesign introduced in steps from January 2027, with completion charted by index-case month cohorts through December 2027.
response.population: All contacts of pulmonary tuberculosis cases notified by the program; baseline cohorts from January to December 2026, improvement cohorts from January to December 2027.
response.exposure: Redesigned pathway: blood draw at the first home visit (with courier pickup), results routed directly to the case nurse, chest X-ray booked at the result visit, interpreters booked for every step, and a standard work checklist for closing each contact.
response.procedures: A mapping team of two nurses, a clinic phlebotomist, a central office clerk and a radiology booker maps the current state with ten recent cases, then the future state. Changes are introduced one at a time, each tested with a small group of cases before spreading. The monthly extract (DS-114) includes identification, test, result, radiograph and closure dates; a missing-date check is run before each chart update.

response.designSummary: Run chart and p-chart of 60-day completion by index-case month cohort: 12 baseline cohorts (2026) and 12 improvement cohorts (2027).
response.sampleSize: About 1,300 contacts a year give cohorts of about 100 contacts per index-case month. With a baseline near 71 percent, p-chart limits for cohorts of 100 are about 14 points either side, so single cohorts can show only large changes, but run chart rules detect a sustained 12-point improvement within five to six cohorts (retrieved simulation). A rise to 85 percent held for six cohorts would meet the shift rule by mid-2027. Equity subgroups (about 15 to 25 contacts a month each) are charted quarterly and described, not tested.
response.primaryAnalysis: Run chart of cohort completion with the baseline median; shift, trend and runs rules fixed in advance; p-chart with 3-sigma limits alongside.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Median days to completed evaluation per cohort; cascade losses per step; nurse hours per case; quarterly completion for shelter, shift-working and interpreter-needing contacts.
response.missingData: Cohorts are charted only after the missing-date check; contacts with a missing closure date after checking are counted as not completed and the number is reported.
response.multiplicity: One aim measure; the rest are descriptive.
response.software: Spreadsheet chart template maintained by the program epidemiologist.
overfittingGuards: Rules and baseline fixed before the first change
No re-baselining until a sustained shift
response.summary: Monthly cohorts of about 100 contacts; a sustained 12-point change detectable within about six cohorts.

response.risks: Low: changes to how an existing public health service is delivered. Home blood draw carries the usual small risks of venepuncture; privacy risk if contact information leaves the program.
response.consent: Contact evaluation is a public health service; contacts consent to each test as now. Program evaluation uses de-identified extracts under the data steward's approval.
response.data: Contact names stay in the case management system; the extract (DS-114) holds dates and contact type only.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people in shelters, shift workers, people needing interpreters and people without a phone are the least likely to complete evaluation. The redesign books interpreters for every step, offers evening home visits and shelter-based blood draws, and reports completion for these groups separately each quarter.
response.effectiveness: Success is a sustained rise to at least 85 percent with no fall for the hardest-to-reach contacts.
response.efficiency: Removes two handoffs and repeated calls; nurse visit time rises.
response.costs: Courier pickups within the existing contract; staff time.
response.partnerships: Shelter staff, a community interpreter service, hospital radiology booking and two people who went through contact evaluation last year.
response.rebPath: Program evaluation under the medical officer of health's approval (MOH-TB-2026-05) with de-identified data; not research requiring REB review, and a publication would follow SQUIRE 2.0.
response.limitations: Before-and-after within one program; radiology booking outside program control.
response.summary: Low-risk service redesign with de-identified evaluation data and equity reporting.

response.partnershipPlan: Two people who went through contact evaluation last year and a shelter worker review the future-state map and the letters to contacts.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comments from the program's contact satisfaction cards are read.

response.title: A Lean redesign of tuberculosis contact evaluation in a city public health program
response.abstract: Problem: 71 percent of contacts completed evaluation within 60 days against a 90 percent target. Intervention: value stream mapping and redesign (home blood draw, direct result routing, same-visit X-ray booking, interpreters at every step). Measures: 60-day completion by index-case month cohort, time to completion, cascade losses, nurse hours and completion for hardest-to-reach contacts. Results will be written after December 2027.
response.introduction: Contact evaluation for tuberculosis loses people at every handoff, most often between a positive test and the radiograph. Lean redesign and home testing improved completion in other programs.
response.methods: Two mapping days produced a future-state map, and changes were introduced one at a time. Completion was charted by index-case month cohort from a checked monthly extract, with rules fixed before the first change.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will show cohort charts with changes marked, cascade losses by step, nurse hours per case and quarterly completion for the hardest-to-reach contacts.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate chart signals to the changes and report equity groups separately. It will state which changes the program keeps.
response.limitations: This is a single program with a before-and-after design. Radiology booking lies outside program control.
response.conclusion: To be written after the last cohort closes. It will report whether the 85 percent aim was met without widening gaps.
